claim: Phasic changes in dopamine level encode the reward prediction error (RPE), which measures the difference between the reward expected after an action and the reward actually received.
source: Phasic changes in dopamine level are believed to encode the reward prediction error (RPE), which measures the difference between the reward expected after an action, and the reward actually received (Schultz et al., 1993, Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schultz et al., 1993 and 1997

claim: The reward prediction error guides reinforcement learning such that behaviour is adapted to changing surroundings.
source: In turn the RPE guides reinforcement learning (RL) such that behaviour is adapted to changing surroundings.
evidence: Based on established understanding in the field

claim: Parkinson's disease involves dopaminergic depletion in the substantia nigra pars compacta and ventral tegmental area.
source: Several studies have taken advantage of the dopaminergic depletion in Parkinson's disease (PD) in the substantia nigra pars compacta and ventral tegmental area (Agid et al., 1989; Shulman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agid et al., 1989 and Shulman et al., 2011

claim: PD patients are frequently treated with dopamine replacement therapy (levodopa and dopamine agonists).
source: PD patients are frequently treated with dopamine replacement therapy (levodopa and dopamine agonists), and thus by comparing patients in ON and OFF medication states the effects of dopamine depletion can be investigated.

claim: Dopaminergic state modulated reinforcement learning from positive and negative feedback in the Frank et al. 2004 study.
source: One influential study using such a procedure found that dopaminergic state modulated RL from positive and negative feedback (Frank et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frank et al., 2004

claim: In the Probabilistic Selection Task, participants see two Japanese Hiragana symbols on the screen at the same time and must pick one, receiving either 'Correct' or 'Incorrect' feedback.
source: This study used the Probabilistic Selection Task (PST), in which participants see two Japanese Hiragana symbols on the screen at the same time, and must pick one, receiving either 'Correct' or 'Incorrect' feedback (see Figure 1).
evidence: Description of the task procedure with reference to Figure 1

claim: In the PST, feedback is determined probabilistically, with card A in pair AB given positive feedback on 80% of trials and negative feedback on 20%.
source: This feedback is determined probabilistically, so that card A in pair AB is given positive feedback on 80% of trials, and negative feedback on 20%, and vice versa for card B.

claim: Pairs CD and EF in the PST have reward probabilities of 70-30% and 60-40%, respectively.
source: Pairs CD and EF have probabilities 70–30% and 60–40%, respectively.

claim: PD patients chose A more and avoided B less when ON medication in the Frank et al. 2004 study.
source: PD patients chose A more and avoided B less when ON medication, and vice versa for OFF medication (Frank et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frank et al., 2004

claim: PD patients OFF medication were better at negative reinforcement than healthy age-matched controls in the Frank et al. 2004 study.
source: Importantly, patients OFF medication were better at negative reinforcement than healthy age-matched controls (HC), suggesting that PD actually improved some aspect of RL.
evidence: Supported by citation to Frank et al., 2004

claim: The direct pathway from the striatum is mainly activated by striatal neurons containing dopamine D1 receptors and is activated by a dopamine increase during a positive RPE.
source: The direct pathway, which is mainly activated by striatal neurons containing dopamine D1 receptors and therefore is activated by a dopamine increase during a positive RPE, underlies positive reinforcement.
evidence: Based on the Go-NoGo model of basal ganglia function

claim: The indirect pathway is inhibited by D2 receptors and is activated when a dopamine decrease signals a negative RPE.
source: The indirect pathway which is inhibited by D2 receptors, and therefore activated when a dopamine decrease signals a negative RPE, allows negative reinforcement.
evidence: Based on the Go-NoGo model of basal ganglia function

claim: When PD patients are ON medication, higher dopamine levels activate D1 receptors and inhibit D2 receptors, thus biasing towards the direct pathway and improving positive reinforcement.
source: When PD patients are ON medication, the higher dopamine levels activate D1 receptors and inhibit D2 receptors, thus biasing towards the direct pathway, improving positive reinforcement.

claim: When PD patients are OFF medication, lower dopamine levels mean less D1 activation and less D2 inhibition, thus increasing indirect pathway activity and improving negative reinforcement.
source: When OFF medication, the lower dopamine levels mean less D1 activation, and less D2 inhibition, thus increasing indirect pathway activity, and improving negative reinforcement.

claim: Being ON medication at the time of testing produced greater expression of positive reinforcement than being OFF in the Shiner et al. 2012 study.
source: It was found that being ON medication at the time of testing produced greater expression of positive reinforcement than being OFF, while it had no effect during learning.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shiner et al., 2012

claim: RPE signals in the striatum during learning were not affected by medication state in the Shiner et al. 2012 study.
source: Additionally, RPE signals in the striatum during learning were not affected by medication state, but ventromedial PFC and nucleus accumbens signals in the test phase only tracked the value of the stimuli when patients were ON medication.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shiner et al., 2012

claim: Dopaminergic effects could be shown even when rewards were not actually given during learning in the Smittenaar et al. 2012 study.
source: The direct link between dopamine and RL, as opposed to expression of information, was further questioned by another study, which found that dopaminergic effects could be shown even when rewards were not actually given during learning (Smittenaar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smittenaar et al., 2012

claim: PD patients ON medication during testing showed higher accuracy on the most rewarded stimulus and lower accuracy on the most punished stimulus in the Smittenaar et al. 2012 study.
source: However, they still found that PD patients ON medication during testing (after finding out about the money), showed higher accuracy on the most rewarded stimulus, and lower accuracy on the most punished stimulus.
evidence: Supported by citation to Smittenaar et al., 2012

claim: PD patients ON medication showed an increase in accuracy on an RL task after a 20 min delay in the Coulthard et al. 2012 study.
source: PD patients ON medication showed an increase in accuracy on an RL task after a 20 min delay, while those OFF medication showed a large decrease (Coulthard et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coulthard et al., 2012

claim: All PD patients showed the same behaviour during the learning trials in the Coulthard et al. 2012 study.
source: This was despite all PD patients showing the same behaviour during the learning trials.
evidence: Supported by citation to Coulthard et al., 2012

claim: Dopamine is hypothesised to set the threshold for the synthesis of plasticity-related proteins (PRPs).
source: Dopamine is hypothesised to set the threshold for the synthesis of these PRPs, so that higher levels of dopamine mean a lower threshold.
evidence: Based on synaptic tagging and capture hypothesis models

claim: PD patients OFF medication would have a higher PRP threshold and therefore lower consolidation of early synaptic changes, leading to a delayed impairment of memory.
source: Thus, PD patients OFF medication would have a higher PRP threshold, and therefore lower consolidation of early synaptic changes, leading to a delayed impairment of memory, as seen in Coulthard et al. (2012).
evidence: Inference from synaptic tagging and capture hypothesis

claim: Eighteen PD patients and 18 HC learned a modified version of the PST in experiment 1.
source: Eighteen PD patients and 18 HC learned a modified version of the PST (2 pairs, different probabilities of reward, smiling or frowning faces as feedback, see Figure 7), and were tested immediately, 30 min and 24 hr later.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure with reference to Figure 7

claim: PD patients were ON or OFF their dopaminergic medication on day 1 during learning, and ON or OFF on day 2 for testing (4 conditions; within-subject design) in experiment 1.
source: PD patients were ON or OFF their dopaminergic medication on day 1 during learning, and ON or OFF on day 2 for testing (4 conditions; within-subject design).

claim: Participants were able to learn the task in experiment 1, with final mean accuracies of 78.60% (SEM = 3.84) ON medication, 77.71% (4.16) OFF medication and 79.03% (4.67) for HC.
source: Participants were able to learn the task, with final mean accuracies of 78.60% (SEM = 3.84) ON medication, 77.71% (4.16) OFF medication and 79.03% (4.67) for HC.

claim: A dual learning rate Q-learning model where the learning rates did not differ by medication state provided the best fit in experiment 1.
source: A dual learning rate Q-learning model where the learning rates did not differ by medication state provided the best fit, further suggesting that dopaminergic medication did not affect learning.

claim: Both day 1 OFF conditions (and HC) have mean decreases in memory scores between 30 min and 24 hr, while both day 1 ON conditions have slight increases in mean memory scores in experiment 1.
source: Figure 2 shows that both day 1 OFF conditions (and HC) have mean decreases in memory scores, while both day 1 ON conditions have slight increases in mean memory scores, although the standard error bars overlap with zero for the latter.

claim: There was no significant effect of day 1 medication state on the difference between 24 hr and 30 min memory scores (F (1, 16) = 2.803, p=0.114, ηp2 =0.149) in experiment 1.
source: A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (day 1 medications * day 2 medication) showed no significant effect of day 1 medication state on the difference between 24 hr and 30 min memory scores (F (1, 16) = 2.803, p=0.114, ηp2 =0.149), and no other effects were significant (p>0.3, ηp2 <0.064).

claim: Comparing ON-OFF and OFF-OFF showed significant difference in the change across 24 hr (t (16)=2.894, p=0.0106, d = 0.4959) in experiment 1.
source: Comparing ON-OFF and OFF-OFF showed no difference in the change across 30 min (p=0.292, d = 0.3233), but did show significant difference in the change across 24 hr (t (16)=2.894, p=0.0106, d = 0.4959).

claim: The significant difference between ON-OFF and OFF-OFF in the change across 24 hr survived Bonferroni correction for four comparisons (α = 0.0125) in experiment 1.
source: This survived Bonferroni correction for four comparisons (α = 0.0125).
evidence: Statistical analysis with multiple comparison correction

claim: Low dopamine levels during learning or early memory may affect the persistence of the reinforced memory, at least in certain circumstances.
source: This suggests that low dopamine levels during learning or early memory may affect the persistence of the reinforced memory, at least in certain circumstances.

claim: The overall accuracy on the novel pairs test showed a positive correlation with the accuracy in the final learning block (r = 0.4365, p<0.0001) in experiment 1.
source: The overall accuracy on the novel pairs test showed a positive correlation with the accuracy in the final learning block (r = 0.4365, p<0.0001), which is not surprising as participants who learned the task well would be expected to perform better on the test.

claim: Choose-A and avoid-B were not significantly different between PD patients and HC (p=0.714, d = 0.0969; p=0.753, d = 0.0834) in experiment 1.
source: Choose-A and avoid-B were not significantly different between PD patients and HC (p=0.714, d = 0.0969; p=0.753, d = 0.0834).

claim: There were no effects of dopaminergic state during day 1 or day 2 on expression of positive and negative reinforcement in experiment 1.
source: We found no effects of dopaminergic state during day 1 or day 2 on expression of positive and negative reinforcement.

claim: There were no significant effects of day 1 or day 2 medication state, or any interactions (p>0.12) in the repeated measures ANOVA in experiment 1.
source: There were no significant effects of day 1 or day 2 medication state, or any interactions (p>0.12).

claim: Overall PD patients were better at expressing negative reinforcement, but medication on day 1 or day 2 had no effect in experiment 1.
source: This suggests that overall PD patients were better at expressing negative reinforcement, but that medication on day 1 or day 2 had no effect.

claim: Neither day 1 nor day 2 medication state affected choose-A or avoid-B performance in experiment 1.
source: This suggests that neither day 1 nor day 2 medication state affected choose-A or avoid-B performance.

claim: No significant effects of choice or medication state were seen on the filtered data (p>0.1) in experiment 1.
source: No significant effects of choice or medication state were seen on the filtered data (p>0.1; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis of filtered experimental data

claim: There were no significant effects of medication or disease state in experiment 1, suggesting that PD and dopaminergic medication did not affect novel pairs performance on the modified PST when tested 24 hr later.
source: Overall, there were no significant effects of medication or disease state, suggesting that PD and dopaminergic medication did not affect novel pairs performance on the modified PST when tested 24 hr later.

claim: Eighteen PD patients and 20 HC completed the modified PST with the novel pairs test immediately after learning in experiment 2.
source: Eighteen PD patients and 20 HC completed the modified PST with the novel pairs test immediately after learning.

claim: Overall accuracy in the novel pairs tests correlated positively with accuracy in the final learning block (r = 0.6686, p<0.0001) in experiment 2.
source: Overall accuracy in the novel pairs tests correlated positively with accuracy in the final learning block (r = 0.6686, p<0.0001).

claim: A multivariate ANOVA comparing PD patients and HC showed no effects of disease state on choose-A (p=0.285, ηp2 = 0.021) or avoid-B (p=0.226, ηp2 = 0.027) in experiment 2.
source: A multivariate ANOVA comparing PD patients and HC showed no effects of disease state on choose-A (p=0.285, ηp2 = 0.021) or avoid-B (p=0.226, ηp2 = 0.027).

claim: Paired samples t-tests to compare ON and OFF medication conditions showed no significant differences for choose-A (p=0.727, d = 0.1311) or avoid-B (p=0.580, d = 0.1910) in experiment 2.
source: Paired samples t-tests to compare ON and OFF medication conditions showed no significant differences for choose-A (p=0.727, d = 0.1311) or avoid-B (p=0.580, d = 0.1910; Figure 4a).

claim: No effects of condition were found in the filtered data (p>0.1) in experiment 2.
source: Filtered data were also analysed; 1/18 ON, 3/18 OFF and 3/20 HC blocks were filtered out, and no effects of condition were found (p>0.1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of filtered experimental data

claim: Experiment 2 did not find evidence that dopaminergic medication state affects choices on the modified-PST.
source: Thus we did not find evidence that dopaminergic medication state affects choices on the modified-PST as in previous studies (Frank et al., 2004).

claim: Eighteen PD patients and 18 HC completed the original PST in experiment 3.
source: Eighteen PD patients and 18 HC completed the original PST (Frank et al., 2004).

claim: The final learning accuracies in experiment 3 were lower than in experiments 1 and 2.
source: Note that the final learning accuracies were lower than in experiments 1 and 2.
evidence: Comparison of experimental data across experiments

claim: Overall accuracy in the novel pairs test correlated positively with the accuracy in the final learning block (r = 0.4680, p=0.0004) in experiment 3.
source: Again, overall accuracy in the novel pairs test correlated positively with the accuracy in the final learning block (r = 0.4680, p=0.0004).

claim: Paired-samples t-tests showed no significant differences in choose-A (p=0.363, d = 0.2573) or avoid-B selections for the two medication conditions (p=0.968, d = 0.0132) in experiment 3.
source: Paired-samples t-tests showed no significant differences in choose-A (p=0.363, d = 0.2573) or avoid-B selections for the two medication conditions (p=0.968, d = 0.0132), meaning dopaminergic medication state didn't affect positive or negative reinforcement in PD patients (Figure 4b).

claim: Dopaminergic medication state didn't affect positive or negative reinforcement in PD patients in experiment 3.
source: Paired-samples t-tests showed no significant differences in choose-A (p=0.363, d = 0.2573) or avoid-B selections for the two medication conditions (p=0.968, d = 0.0132), meaning dopaminergic medication state didn't affect positive or negative reinforcement in PD patients (Figure 4b).

claim: No significant effects of disease or medication were seen in the filtered data (p>0.5) in experiment 3.
source: Data filtering excluded 8/18 ON blocks, 6/18 OFF blocks and 7/18 HC blocks, and no significant effects of disease or medication were seen in the remaining data (p>0.5; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis of filtered experimental data

claim: Participants were only just above chance performance on the novel pairs task in experiment 3, with mean percentage of choices between 49% and 57% for all groups.
source: It should be noted that participants were only just above chance performance on the novel pairs task in experiment 3, with mean percentage of choices between 49% and 57% for all groups.
evidence: Experimental data from novel pairs test

claim: Performance in experiment 3 was lower than in experiments 1 and 2, suggesting that the original PST was harder for participants to learn.
source: This is lower than in experiments 1 and 2, suggesting that the original PST was harder for participants to learn.
evidence: Inference from comparison of experimental data

claim: A univariate analysis showed a significant effect of experiment (F (2, 187)=18.416, p<0.000001, ηp2 =0.165) on final learning block accuracies.
source: A univariate analysis was run on the final learning block accuracies for each experiment (Figure 5), which showed a significant effect of experiment (F (2, 187)=18.416, p<0.000001, ηp2 =0.165), but no effects of condition (p=0.578, ηp2=0.015) or interaction (p=0.587, ηp2 = 0.015).
evidence: Statistical analysis of combined experimental data

claim: There were no effects of condition (p=0.578, ηp2=0.015) or interaction (p=0.587, ηp2 = 0.015) on final learning block accuracies across experiments.
source: A univariate analysis was run on the final learning block accuracies for each experiment (Figure 5), which showed a significant effect of experiment (F (2, 187)=18.416, p<0.000001, ηp2 =0.165), but no effects of condition (p=0.578, ηp2=0.015) or interaction (p=0.587, ηp2 = 0.015).
evidence: Statistical analysis of combined experimental data

claim: Post-hoc comparisons with Bonferroni corrections showed that experiment 3 had significantly lower final learning block accuracies than experiments 1 (p<0.000001) and 2 (p=0.000002).
source: Post-hoc comparisons with Bonferroni corrections showed that experiment 3 had significantly lower final learning block accuracies than experiments 1 (p<0.000001) and 2 (p=0.000002), but there were no differences between experiments 1 and 2 (p=1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of combined experimental data

claim: There were no differences between experiments 1 and 2 in final learning block accuracies (p=1).
source: Post-hoc comparisons with Bonferroni corrections showed that experiment 3 had significantly lower final learning block accuracies than experiments 1 (p<0.000001) and 2 (p=0.000002), but there were no differences between experiments 1 and 2 (p=1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of combined experimental data

claim: Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc tests showed that experiment 3 had lower avoid-B than experiments 1 (p=0.000005) and 2 (p=0.000013), while experiments 1 and 2 did not differ (p=1).
source: Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc tests showed that experiment 3 had lower avoid-B than experiments 1 (p=0.000005) and 2 (p=0.000013), while experiments 1 and 2 did not differ (p=1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of combined experimental data

claim: Experiment 3 had poorer final learning accuracy (despite passing the accuracy thresholds) and less avoid-B choices on the novel pairs test than experiments 1 and 2 which used the modified-PST.
source: This means that experiment 3 had poorer final learning accuracy (despite passing the accuracy thresholds) and less avoid-B choices on the novel pairs test, than experiments 1 and 2 which used the modified-PST.
evidence: Summary of statistical comparisons across experiments

claim: Experiments 1 and 2 had avoid-B scores higher than choose-A, while experiment 3 had about the same scores.
source: Interestingly, this was because experiments 1 and 2 had avoid-B scores higher than choose-A, while experiment 3 had about the same scores.

claim: Dopaminergic medication during learning prevented a decrease in memory for RL over 24 hr.
source: These experiments found that dopaminergic medication during learning prevented a decrease in memory for RL over 24 hr.

claim: Dopamine did not affect expression of positive or negative reinforcement either during learning or testing, when tested immediately or 24 hr after learning.
source: However, dopamine did not affect expression of positive or negative reinforcement either during learning or testing, when tested immediately or 24 hr after learning.

claim: PD patients did not differ from HC in any of the experiments.
source: PD patients did not differ from HC in any of the experiments.

claim: Experiment 3, using the original PST, had much lower accuracy in the learning trials and lower avoid-B scores than experiments 1 and 2 which used the modified-PST.
source: Finally, experiment 3, using the original PST, had much lower accuracy in the learning trials, and lower avoid-B scores than experiments 1 and 2 which used the modified-PST.

claim: Day 1 dopamine improved consolidation of the learned values sometime after 30 min, preventing a decay in the memory.
source: As this score was the difference between 30 min and 24 hr delay tests, it suggests that day 1 dopamine improved consolidation of the learned values sometime after 30 min, preventing a decay in the memory.

claim: All PD patients went back ON medication immediately after the day 1 session regardless of day 2 condition, so all patients were in an ON state for the hours after learning.
source: All PD patients went back ON medication immediately after the day 1 session regardless of day 2 condition, so all patients were in an ON state for the hours after learning (see Figure 6 for diagram).

claim: The day 1 ON and OFF groups differed in dopaminergic activity until about 1.5 hr after learning, when the medication would have reached peak concentration.
source: This means the day 1 ON and OFF groups differed in dopaminergic activity until about 1.5 hr after learning, when the medication would have reached peak concentration.
evidence: Inference from experimental procedure and pharmacokinetics

claim: There is a short time window for day 1 medication to affect consolidation of RL.
source: This gives a short time window for day 1 medication to affect consolidation of RL.

claim: Dopamine given before or after learning can improve consolidation.
source: Dopamine given before or after learning can improve consolidation (Bernabeu et al., 1997; de Lima et al., 2011; Furini et al., 2014; Péczely et al., 2016; Rossato et al., 2009), although there is still debate on the time course of its effects.

claim: Synaptic tagging and capture models suggest dopaminergic effects would take place within a few hours of learning.
source: Synaptic tagging and capture models suggest dopaminergic effects would take place within a few hours of learning (Clopath et al., 2008; Redondo and Morris, 2011), and consolidation effects on RL have been reported over shorter times before (Coulthard et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claim: The PST is assumed to rely on basal ganglia functioning, at least when there are short delays between action and feedback.
source: However, the PST is assumed to rely on basal ganglia functioning, at least when there are short delays between action and feedback as there were here (Foerde and Shohamy, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Foerde and Shohamy, 2011

claim: Sleep affects performance on the Weather Prediction Task.
source: Three studies have found that sleep affects performance on the Weather Prediction Task (Barsky et al., 2015; Djonlagic et al., 2009; Lerner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to three studies

claim: Dopamine has been shown to affect sleep consolidation for reward-related memory.
source: Dopamine has also been shown to affect sleep consolidation for reward-related memory (Feld et al., 2014), and while reward-related memory is partly a declarative memory process, it relies on the same reward-processing brain regions that underlie RL (Wittmann et al., 2005).

claim: Dopamine has been implicated in reconsolidation.
source: Dopamine has been implicated in reconsolidation (Rossato et al., 2015), although it has not been investigated in the RL domain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossato et al., 2015

claim: The direction of effect in experiment 1 was opposite to the expected effect, with the day 1 ON conditions having the highest amount of avoid-B selections.
source: Interestingly, the direction of effect was opposite to the expected effect, with the day 1 ON conditions having the highest amount of avoid-B selections.

claim: The average accuracy on novel pairs in experiment 3 was much lower than reported in Frank et al. (2004), where patients ON medications achieved 78% accuracy in choosing A and patients OFF medications achieved 82% accuracy in avoiding B.
source: The average accuracy on novel pairs in experiment 3 was much lower than reported in Frank et al. (2004), where the patients ON medications achieved 78% accuracy in choosing A and patients OFF medications achieved 82% accuracy in avoiding B.

claim: The corresponding accuracies in experiment 3 were very close to chance (53% and 51%, respectively; 54.5% and 46.7% for filtered data).
source: By contrast the corresponding accuracies in our experiment were very close to chance (53% and 51%, respectively; 54.5% and 46.7% for filtered data).

claim: The samples in the current study were very closely matched in age, gender and disease severity to the PD patients tested ON medication in Frank et al. (2004).
source: Our samples were very closely matched in age, gender and disease severity to the PD patients tested ON medication in Frank et al. (2004).

claim: T-tests on the Frank et al. (2004) PD sample and the experiment 3 sample showed no significant differences in ages or Hoehn and Yahr stages.
source: T-tests on the Frank et al. (2004) PD sample and our experiment 3 sample showed no significant differences in ages or Hoehn and Yahr stages, and χ2 tests showed no significant difference in gender distributions between PD and HC (p>0.1).

claim: The PD patients (p<0.001) and HC (p=0.046) in experiment 3 had fewer years of education on average than those in Frank et al. (2004).
source: The PD patients (p<0.001) and HC (p=0.046) in experiment 3 had fewer years of education on average than those in Frank et al. (2004), which could have contributed to the failure to learn this task, although our experiment 1 sample also had fewer years of education (p<0.001) and they could learn the modified PST.

claim: Higher dopamine levels either improve expression of positive reinforcement or impair negative reinforcement or both in multiple studies.
source: Many studies have used the PST (or variations), and while the findings are not always exactly the same, the general pattern of higher dopamine levels either improving expression of positive reinforcement (Rutledge et al., 2009; Shiner et al., 2012; Smittenaar et al., 2012; Voon et al., 2010), impairing negative reinforcement (Cools et al., 2006; Frank et al., 2007b; Mathar et al., 2017), or both (Bódi et al., 2009; Maril et al., 2013; Palminteri et al., 2009; Piray et al., 2014; Wittmann et al., 2005; Voon et al., 2010) has been seen multiple times.

claim: Low dopamine conditions have shown either worse positive reinforcement, better negative reinforcement, or both in multiple studies.
source: Likewise, low dopamine conditions have shown either worse positive reinforcement (Eisenegger et al., 2014; Jocham et al., 2011; Kobza et al., 2012), better negative reinforcement (Bódi et al., 2009; Cox et al., 2015; Frank et al., 2004; Voon et al., 2010), or both (Palminteri et al., 2009; Piray et al., 2014).

claim: PD patients with greater left hemisphere pathology showed dopaminergic medication modulated reward and punishment learning, while patients with greater right hemisphere pathology showed no such effects in the Maril et al. 2013 study.
source: One study found that while PD patients with greater left hemisphere pathology showed dopaminergic medication modulated reward and punishment learning, patients with greater right hemisphere pathology showed no such effects (Maril et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maril et al., 2013

claim: Left-hemisphere patients are more common and are likely to be over-represented in study samples unless specifically balanced.
source: They also pointed out that left-hemisphere patients are more common, so are likely to be over-represented in study samples unless specifically balanced.

claim: The PST was found to have low test-retest reliability when retested 7-8 weeks later in the Baker et al. 2013 study.
source: Additionally, the PST was found to have low test-retest reliability when retested 7–8 weeks later (Baker et al., 2013); as well as low correlation between performance at different time points, participants initially classed as 'positive learners' or 'negative learners' were labelled differently when retested.
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2013

claim: The Baker et al. 2013 study failed to find any effects of several dopaminergic genes on RL, in contradiction to previous genetic studies.
source: The study also failed to find any effects of several dopaminergic genes on RL, in contradiction to previous genetic studies (Doll et al., 2011; Frank and Hutchison, 2009; Frank et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2013 and comparison with other cited studies

claim: Performance on the PST depends on the discriminability of the stimuli used, with the difference in discriminability of stimuli A vs B and stimuli C vs D affecting whether healthy participants showed choose-A or avoid-B biases.
source: A recent study has shown that performance on the PST depends on the discriminability of the stimuli used, with the difference in discriminability of stimuli A vs B, and stimuli C vs D affecting whether healthy participants showed choose-A or avoid-B biases (Schutte et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schutte et al., 2017

claim: Small changes such as changes to the stimuli used or changing the delay between action and feedback can have large effects on how the PST works.
source: Small changes such as changes to the stimuli used, or changing the delay between action and feedback can have large effects on how this task works (Foerde and Shohamy, 2011; Schutte et al., 2017).

claim: Small modifications to RL task procedure can have large effects on behaviour.
source: Care should be taken when comparing across such procedures, as we, and others, have shown that small modifications to RL task procedure can have large effects on behaviour.
evidence: Inference from current study and cited literature

claim: Dopaminergic neurons activate striatal D1 neurons, which are believed to be involved in activating movements, while they inhibit the D2 neurons, which are thought to be involved in movement inhibition.
source: In particular, how our results can be reconciled with the observations that dopaminergic neurons activate striatal D1 neurons, which are believed to be involved in activating movements, while they inhibit the D2 neurons, which are thought to be involved in movement inhibition (Kravitz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kravitz et al., 2010

claim: D1 and D2 neurons encode not only the expected value of an action in the difference of their activity, but also the variance of the reward in the sum of their activity according to the Mikhael and Bogacz 2016 model.
source: It has been recently proposed that these neurons encode not only the expected value of an action in the difference of their activity, but also the variance of the reward in the sum of their activity (Mikhael and Bogacz, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mikhael and Bogacz, 2016

claim: In PST simulations, stimuli with reward probability closer to 50% strongly activated both D1 and D2 neurons.
source: In PST, the stimuli with reward probability closer to 50% have a high variance of reward, because on some trials they result in positive and on some trials in negative feedback. In the simulations of the PST these stimuli strongly activated both D1 and D2 neurons (Mikhael and Bogacz, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mikhael and Bogacz, 2016

claim: Dopamine and PD did not affect expression of positive or negative reinforcement when tested immediately or 24 hr after learning in the current study.
source: Dopamine and PD did not affect expression of positive or negative reinforcement when tested immediately or 24 hr after learning.

claim: Dopamine during learning improved the consolidation of RL memories over 24 hr in the current study.
source: Dopamine during learning improved the consolidation of RL memories over 24 hr.

claim: The original PST had very low accuracy in the current study.
source: The original PST had very low accuracy, and the modifications made to the PST had large effects, increasing learning and novel pairs accuracy, and increasing the amount of avoid-B selections participants made.

claim: The modifications made to the PST had large effects, increasing learning and novel pairs accuracy, and increasing the amount of avoid-B selections participants made.
source: The original PST had very low accuracy, and the modifications made to the PST had large effects, increasing learning and novel pairs accuracy, and increasing the amount of avoid-B selections participants made.

claim: These experiments failed to replicate the previously reported effects of dopamine and PD on RL, suggesting the effect may be weak.
source: These experiments failed to replicate the previously reported effects of dopamine and PD on RL, suggesting the effect may be weak.
